newsitem.title: FRANCE: French farm unions attack EU reform proposal.
newsitem.headline: French farm unions attack EU reform proposal.

text.p: France's largest farm union, the 600,000-member FNSEA, dismissed a European Union farm reform plan unveiled on Wednesday as a "surrender" to the United States and a threat to jobs.

The union said European Commission proposals to cut prices to remain competitive would play into the hands of the United States and other free-market nations ahead of new global trade negotiations slated for the turn of the century.
"Under the pretext of globalisation, the Commission is following the economic liberalism of the Anglo Saxons in a wide-eyed fashion," the broad-based FNSEA said in a statement.
"It surrenders to our American competitors and the Cairns group countries even before negotiations begin," it said.
The Cairns group is a loose assembly of free-trading farming nations led by Australia and New Zealand.

The EU proposals, known as Agenda 2000, reinforce 1992 reforms designed to make EU farmers more competitive by cutting prices towards world levels and shifting support to direct aid which is seen as better for the economy than propping up prices.
The FNSEA said the EU, which plans to expand eastwards, should remain an important world food exporter but not at the expense of its 30-year-old Common Agricultural Policy.
Submitting agriculture to an "accountant" approach would erode family incomes and weaken agricultural employment.
The leftist farm union Confederation Paysanne urged the EU to maintain the principle of "Community preference" which gives its farmers an edge over foreign competition.
"We do not want a CAP which blindly follows the American model," a spokesman said.
The United States last year introduced its most radical farm reforms since the 1930s Depression, known as the Fair Act, to allow its farmers a better chance to compete globally.
Despite this, farm spending was still higher per farmer in the United States than in the EU, the Confederation said.
It said the previous CAP reform, which was opposed in sometimes violent street protests by French farmers, had cost 100,000 jobs since being brought into force in 1993.
